title: Superflow vs Spur
kicker: · SUPERFLOW VS SPUR · THE AI QA REVIEWER WITH A HUMAN IN THE LOOP
headline: Spur is a QA testing platform. Superflow is a QA reviewer + a human in the loop.
secondary: The reviewer is AI agents, built from your QA checklist. They check every site change and pin what they find. Your team makes every call, and every call trains the next review. Sign-off happens from a link, no account needed.
prevents: Stop finding every mistake by hand.
No more manual pass before launch.
qualifier: If you ship work that someone has to approve, not just code that has to pass CI, this page is for you.
heroCaption: The agents find it. Your team calls it. Approval takes one link.

dimensions.label: Who checks the site
dimensions.framing: This is the one place the two genuinely overlap, so take it plainly.
leftFacts: Agents run your checklist. Every change, desktop and mobile.
Broken links, brand colors and fonts against the brand guide, spelling, accessibility basics, and SEO.
Findings land as pinned comments, rationale attached.
rightFacts: Autonomous agents plan, execute, and report tests. Five types: exploratory, localization, UI/UX, functional, and AI feature testing.
The UI/UX agent explores the product like a real user and catches typos, content inconsistencies, layout overflows, and broken interactions.
Written in plain English, no code.
dimensions.verdict: Even, and it says so. Both send an agent instead of a person. The fork is what happens to the finding next.

dimensions.label: How the client says yes
dimensions.framing: Feedback is easy to collect. A yes is harder.
leftFacts: Multi-step review flows: agents check, your team gates, then whoever signs off.
The approver opens a link and taps Approve. No account, no login, no app, from their phone.
rightFacts: Runs report to the team that owns the site, with full video playback and step-level evidence.
An approval or sign-off step for anyone outside that team: none found on spurtest.com.
dimensions.verdict: Spur reports to the team that owns the product. Superflow carries the finding to the person who has to approve the work.

dimensions.label: Where you review
dimensions.framing: Spur drives the product. Superflow lives on the work.
leftFacts: Superflow lives on the site itself: passwords, Okta, SSO, no extension needed, guests included.
Websites plus video, PDFs, images, and Lottie files, reviewed in the same place.
rightFacts: Tests from the outside, like a real user: you provide a URL, and a build file for native apps.
Logins, MFA and OTP handled with test accounts and whitelisted IPs; strict bot protection is worked through with your security team.
Web and native mobile apps only. No PDFs, images, or video review.
dimensions.verdict: Spur goes deeper on one surface, including native iOS and Android. Superflow goes wider, across every format that has to be approved.

dimensions.label: What stays private
dimensions.framing: Your team needs somewhere to disagree.
leftFacts: Internal-only notes your team sees and no one outside it does.
The debate stays private; the approver sees one settled answer.
rightFacts: Every run is internal by construction: results go to your team, and there is no outside view or comment layer.
dimensions.verdict: Not a defect, a consequence. Spur has no outward-facing side, so it has nothing to keep private from one.

dimensions.label: What gets captured
dimensions.framing: Both attach proof without being asked. The proof is a different shape.
leftFacts: Element and text pins, area comments.
A screenshot attaches to every comment automatically.
Recordings: screen, video, voice, from the toolbar.
rightFacts: Every run produces full video playback and step-level evidence.
Their public Bug Book shows the format: test, failure step, screenshot, and cost, rated Critical to Mild.
dimensions.verdict: Spur's video of a failing run is the better proof for an engineer. Superflow's pin on the element is the better proof for whoever has to approve it. Pick by who reads it.

dimensions.label: What it remembers
dimensions.framing: Spur's agents adapt to the site. Superflow's adapt to the brand.
leftFacts: Brand guides, guidelines, and checklists go in once, per brand.
Then your team's calls train it: every accept or reject on an agent's comment teaches that brand's Memory.
The next review starts there. Agents check new work against that brand's rules and past decisions, and Memory flags a likely miss before review even opens.
rightFacts: Intent-based tests adapt when the site changes; when an edit is needed it's plain English, and their team helps.
Learning from a human's accept or reject on a finding, carried into the next run: not yet verified.
dimensions.verdict: Two kinds of adaptation. Spur's tests keep passing when the site changes. Superflow's agents get sharper every time a human overrules one, so what your team rejected last month is what they check for next month.

dimensions.label: How it fits your stack
dimensions.framing: The fix still has to ship.
leftFacts: Two-way Asana, Monday, ClickUp. Slack built in.
rightFacts: CI through GitHub Actions, for example on each pull request.
Spur MCP wires Cursor, Claude, and Copilot to the agent, drafts tests from a pull request diff, and pairs with GitHub, Jira, Linear, or Slack.
Hundreds of tests run in parallel across web and native mobile.
dimensions.verdict: Spur plugs into the release pipeline. Superflow plugs into the delivery workflow. If a pull request is your gate, that's Spur's ground.

pricingCompetitor: Verified August 2026: annual plans based on test-run volume, not per seat. No public price list, no free plan, and no free trial stated; you book a demo for a quote tailored to your release cadence. Most teams start with a one to two week POC, and there is a three-phase pilot program with limited slots. Overages are never auto-billed, they're flagged and agreed together.
switchingLines: One snippet on any site; one click on Webflow, WordPress, or GTM.
Paste the checklist you already have; agents assemble from it.
Nothing has to leave Spur. Its runs gate your release; Superflow gates the sign-off.
honestCloseStrengths: Spur earned its logo wall. Its agents drive real journeys, sign in, checkout with a card, a return, chained together and run hundreds at a time across web, iOS, and Android. Every run comes back with video playback and step-level evidence, and customers report about 80% fewer false positives than scripted suites. Alo spent seven months failing to stabilise Selenium; Spur got tests live in days. Living Spaces went from zero to 80% coverage in a month. Their public Bug Book shows the actual production bugs they caught, with the failing step attached.
stayLine: If the question you need answered is whether the checkout still works, and you have a QA function to own it, Spur is the better tool. Stay.

faq.question: Is Superflow a replacement for Spur?
faq.answer: No, and for a QA team running regression it shouldn't be. Spur automates functional testing for a product team; Superflow runs the review and approval loop for the people shipping the work.

faq.question: Can Superflow test a checkout flow?
faq.answer: Not today. Superflow's agents check pages, they don't simulate multi-step journeys, so a checkout that errors on step three is Spur's catch, not ours.

faq.question: Do the agents replace my reviewers?
faq.answer: No. Agents run the first pass. Your team decides, then whoever owns the sign-off approves.

faq.question: Spur's agents adapt too. How is Superflow's memory different?
faq.answer: Spur's tests adapt to the site, which keeps them passing through a redesign. Superflow's Memory adapts to the brand: every agent comment your team accepts or rejects becomes a rule the next review already checks for.

faq.question: Can we run both?
faq.answer: Yes, and many teams should. Spur gates the release in CI; Superflow gets the campaign page reviewed and signed off.

faq.question: Will reviewers have to learn a new tool?
faq.answer: No. They get a link and an Approve button. No account, no login, no app, from their phone.
